---
title: "Chromatin Disruption in Liver Cancer"
description: "How disruption of chromatin regulation drives hepatocellular carcinoma and cholangiocarcinoma."
image: featured.jpg
---

Liver cancer is the third leading cause of cancer death worldwide, and
hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) accounts for most cases. Its incidence continues
to rise, driven by viral hepatitis, metabolic dysfunction-associated
steatohepatitis, and alcohol-related liver disease. Immune checkpoint inhibitors
are now standard first-line therapy for advanced disease, but fewer than a third
of patients respond and durable benefit is uncommon. Work on why has
concentrated on the immune compartment. We study how the chromatin state of the
tumor cell controls whether the immune system recognizes and kills it.

Chromatin regulators are among the most frequently mutated genes in HCC. The BAF
form of the SWI/SNF remodeling complex alone is disrupted in about one in five
liver tumors, a large genetic subset with no targeted therapy. In most other
cancers, loss of SWI/SNF makes tumors more visible to the immune system and more
responsive to checkpoint blockade. Liver cancer does not follow this pattern. In
our analyses, BAF-mutant tumors have worse survival and do not gain the expected
sensitivity to checkpoint blockade. We think the liver's tolerant immune
environment accounts for the difference, and that mechanisms defined in other
tissues cannot be assumed to hold here.

We are identifying the chromatin regulators that BAF-mutant liver tumors depend
on to maintain these altered states, and testing whether removing them restores
anti-tumor immunity. To keep the tumor and immune system together, we pair
pooled, epigenome-focused CRISPR screens in immunocompetent orthotopic liver
tumors with T-cell killing assays in BAF-mutant liver cancer lines. We want to
find chromatin regulators whose loss reprograms immune-response pathways and to
nominate combinations that could make immunotherapy work in a subtype of liver
cancer that has few options.
